title: The TLS Handshake
summary: Exactly how a TLS session gets established, the symmetric/asymmetric key-exchange split, forward secrecy, and what changed in TLS 1.3.

slides.markdown:
TLS delivers three specific guarantees on top of plain TCP: **confidentiality** (an eavesdropper can't read the content), **integrity** (tampering in transit is detectable), and **authentication** (you can verify you're talking to the real server, via its certificate).

HTTPS is simply HTTP riding on top of this — see [HTTPS — HTTP over TLS](https-tls-in-http) for what that combination means for a browser session specifically.

**Symmetric** encryption uses one shared key for both encrypting and decrypting — fast, but you need a safe way to agree on that key first. **Asymmetric** encryption uses a public/private key pair — no shared secret needed in advance, but far too slow for bulk data.

TLS uses both, each for what it's good at: asymmetric crypto solves the *hard problem* (agreeing on a secret over an untrusted channel), then hands off to fast symmetric crypto for the actual data.

slides.sectionTitle: The TLS 1.2 handshake, step by step
slides.markdown:
`ClientHello` (supported ciphers, a random value) → `ServerHello` + certificate + chosen cipher → key exchange material → both sides derive the same symmetric session key → `Finished` messages confirming it all matches.

![TLS 1.2 handshake from ClientHello to Finished](assets/tls12-handshake.svg)

That's **two full round trips** before any application data moves — the cost TLS 1.3 specifically set out to cut down, covered a few slides ahead.

assets.alt: TLS 1.2 handshake from ClientHello to Finished

slides.sectionTitle: Certificates and the chain of trust
slides.markdown:
A server presents a **leaf certificate**, signed by an **intermediate CA**, itself signed by a **root CA** your browser already trusts. Verifying the chain means walking up signatures until you hit a trusted root.

![Certificate chain from leaf to intermediate to root CA](assets/cert-chain-of-trust.svg)

This layering exists so the root CA's most sensitive key rarely gets used directly. See [Certificates & PKI](certificates-pki) for the full model.

assets.alt: Certificate chain from leaf to intermediate to root CA

slides.markdown:
Older TLS could exchange the session key by having the client **encrypt a random secret with the server's public RSA key** — simple, but if the server's private key is ever compromised, every *past* recorded session using it can be decrypted retroactively.

**Diffie-Hellman (DH)** instead lets both sides compute a shared secret from exchanged public values, without ever transmitting the secret itself — and critically, it can be done with fresh, throwaway keys each time, which is exactly what forward secrecy needs.

**Forward secrecy** means: if an attacker later steals the server's long-term private key, they still can't decrypt *past* recorded traffic, because each session used a unique, temporary (**ephemeral**) key that was never stored anywhere and is gone after the session ends.

This is why modern TLS defaults to **ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (DHE/ECDHE)** rather than static RSA key exchange — it converts "steal one key, read all history" into "steal one key, read nothing extra."

slides.sectionTitle: Symmetric session keys for bulk traffic
slides.markdown:
Once the handshake agrees on a shared secret, TLS derives a **symmetric session key** and switches to a fast symmetric cipher (like AES-GCM or ChaCha20) for the actual HTTP traffic — encrypting gigabytes of data with asymmetric crypto would be computationally prohibitive.

This handoff — expensive asymmetric crypto once, cheap symmetric crypto for everything after — is the same divide-and-conquer pattern behind essentially every secure protocol, not just TLS.

| | TLS 1.2 | TLS 1.3 |
|---|---|---|
| Round trips before data | 2 | 1 |
| Cipher negotiation | Broad legacy list (some weak) | Small curated list, weak ciphers removed |
| Key exchange | RSA or (EC)DHE, RSA still allowed | (EC)DHE only — forward secrecy mandatory |

TLS 1.3 guesses the server's likely cipher choice in the first message itself, cutting a full round trip — and simply removes the legacy, breakable ciphers instead of allowing them as a fallback.

For a server you've already connected to recently, TLS 1.3 supports **0-RTT**: the client sends encrypted application data in its *very first* message, using a key derived from the previous session — no waiting for a fresh handshake at all.

The trade-off: that first 0-RTT message can be **replayed** by an attacker who captured it, since there's no fresh randomness from the server yet to prevent a resend. This is why 0-RTT is typically restricted to idempotent requests (like a `GET`), never something like a payment.

A server hosting many HTTPS sites on one IP needs to know **which** certificate to present before the connection is even encrypted — that's what **SNI (Server Name Indication)** does: the client includes the target hostname, in plaintext, in its very first `ClientHello`.

The catch: because it's sent before encryption starts, SNI is visible to anyone observing the network — which hostname you're connecting to leaks even over an otherwise fully encrypted connection. See [Reverse Proxies & API Gateways](reverse-proxies-gateways).

Side by side: TLS 1.2 needs `ClientHello → ServerHello+cert → key exchange → Finished` across two round trips before data flows. TLS 1.3 collapses this to one — the client guesses parameters in its first message, and the server can often respond with everything needed in a single reply.

![TLS 1.2 two-round-trip handshake compared to TLS 1.3 one-round-trip handshake](assets/tls12-vs-tls13.svg)

On a connection with 100ms round-trip time, that's roughly 100ms shaved off *every single new connection* — a meaningful, measurable win at scale.

assets.alt: TLS 1.2 two-round-trip handshake compared to TLS 1.3 one-round-trip handshake

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: treating handshake latency as free
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "TLS just adds a bit of CPU overhead for encryption — the connection setup itself doesn't really matter for performance."

**Why it's wrong:** the handshake's *round trips* are the real cost, not the crypto math — on a slow or long-distance connection, 1-2 extra round trips can add hundreds of milliseconds before a single byte of actual content arrives.

**Correct model:** minimize round trips deliberately — use TLS 1.3, enable session resumption, and reuse connections (keep-alive) so the handshake cost is paid once per session, not once per request.
